question: How should the preferences of younger investors shape Edward Jones's offerings?

claims.text: The 2025 10-K (published 2026-03-13) lists "changing client demographics, preferences and values" and "changing client expectations for expanded product offerings and technology needs" among the factors that may adversely affect the Partnership's ability to compete and adapt its business model, alongside generational wealth transfer. The filing does not break these preferences out by age.

A BofA Private Bank study (published 2024-06-18) of wealthy Americans reports that 72% of younger investors (ages 21-43) believe above-average returns are no longer possible from traditional stocks and bonds alone, against 28% of investors over 44. Among younger high-net-worth investors, 47% of portfolios are in stocks and bonds versus 74% for older investors, and 17% are in alternatives versus 5%. 93% plan to allocate more to alternatives, and 49% own crypto. This is a wealthy-investor survey, not Edward Jones clients.

The FINRA Foundation investor study (published 2025-12-04) finds investors aged 18-34 much more likely to own individual stocks than mutual funds (82% vs 47%). It also finds them much more likely than older investors to have an options account and to have traded options. Half or more of those under 35 say they invest for social responsibility, entertainment and social activity reasons, though enthusiasm for these has declined noticeably relative to 2021. This is a general US investor survey, not Edward Jones clients.

A BofA Private Bank study (published 2026-06-17) defines younger investors as Gen Z and Millennials aged 21 to 45. It reports that 67% believe traditional stocks and bonds can no longer deliver above-average returns. Younger investors allocate more to alternatives (15%) and crypto (13%) than older investors, and 88% say they are likely to allocate more to alternatives in the next few years. This is a wealthy-investor survey, not Edward Jones clients.

The 2025 10-K (published 2026-03-13) says the Partnership is investing in initiatives to meet clients' planning, investing, saving, spending, borrowing and comprehensive needs. These include recently launched Financial Planning Services, where clients get a more personalized experience with additional planning capabilities. The 10-K also lists targeted client initiatives: High Net Worth, Workplace, and "a new digital platform, focused on attracting and retaining Next Generation investors." The filing says it cannot reliably predict the timing or outcome of these initiatives and that their success depends on broad adoption by advisors, CSTPs and home office associates.

The 2025 10-K (published 2026-03-13) describes the existing offering as investment advisory programs, brokerage and retirement accounts, cash and lending solutions and financial planning offerings, delivered through branch teams. Its Digital and Data division is described as providing new tools so branch teams can hold deeper discovery conversations and give more comprehensive advice and planning.

InvestmentNews (trade press, 2026-08-18, indicative only) reports that Edward Jones took a minority stake in the personal finance app Quicken. The stated intention is to integrate Quicken's personal financial management capabilities into Edward Jones to support its value proposition and advisor conversations. The article notes Edward Jones is still determining where and how Quicken will be offered to clients. The article does not tie the move to younger clients.

WealthManagement.com (trade press, 2026-09-30, indicative only) reports that Edward Jones is developing, with Aboon and Retirement Plan Advisory Group, an end-to-end retirement plan technology platform for advisors serving business owners and their employees. The prospecting module is in beta, and the article says it is expected to go live to the broader network early next year. This relates to the Workplace initiative; the article does not mention younger clients.

Management attributes the decline in net new assets in 2025 partly to an aging client base and generational wealth transfers outside the firm. The 2Q25 10-Q (published 2025-08-08) says net new assets fell 10% in the quarter and 8% in the first half, and that the decrease was attributable to existing clients. The 3Q25 10-Q (published 2025-11-07) says that for the first nine months net new assets fell 4%, with outflows following "an increasing downward trend" influenced by an aging client base and generational wealth transfers outside the firm.

The 10-Q tables (published 2025-08-08 and 2025-11-07) report net new households of 27,000 vs 60,000 in 2Q25 and 77,000 vs 124,000 for the first half. For 3Q25 they report 24,000 vs 53,000, and 101,000 vs 177,000 for the first nine months. Client households were 6.7 million at period end against 6.5 million a year earlier. Net new households are defined as new households opened less households closed. The filings do not split them by age.

The 1Q26 10-Q (published 2026-05-07) reports 6.8 million client households at period end versus 6.6 million a year earlier, and net new assets up 4%. The 2Q26 10-Q (published 2026-08-07) reports net new assets up 6% in the quarter and in the first half, and $2.6 trillion of client assets under care. No age breakdown is given.

The 2025 10-K (published 2026-03-13) names competition for clients in light of generational wealth transfer and changing client demographics, preferences and values as among its most notable strategic risks. It says it addresses them through initiatives to deliver enhanced value and impact for current and potential clients.

The 2025 10-K (published 2026-03-13) describes intense competition from broker-dealers, registered investment advisors, banks, insurers and other firms. It names firms offering enhanced digital experiences, AI and lower cost computer-based "robo-advice." It also names discount firms, including major brokerages offering zero commissions on stocks and ETFs, and "fintech" companies with internet- and mobile-based platforms. It adds that clients can transfer their business at any time and that failing to meet client needs could cause the Partnership to lose clients.

The 2025 10-K (published 2026-03-13) says industry change has required and is expected to continue to require significant investments in financial advisors and other human capital, technology infrastructure, digital initiatives, knowledge- and data-powered tools and strategic relationships. Its stated response includes the new digital platform for Next Generation investors. It also flags that deploying new digital tools is expected to raise exposure to fraud risk.

The 2Q25 and 3Q25 10-Qs (published 2025-08-08 and 2025-11-07) describe a multi-tiered initiative called "Enterprise Reimagined." Management says it is intended to create more efficient operations and deliver more value and a better client experience, in line with a strategic ambition to improve financial wellness for tens of millions of long-term investors. The excerpts do not link it specifically to digital competitors or younger investors.

The evidence above only provides objective context for the strategic question asked. Whether or how Edward Jones should act is a judgment for the strategy team to make, beyond the scope of this evidence engine.

adjacent.text: On Schwab's 3Q26 call (October 2026), the CEO said approximately 70% of new-to-firm retail households are Gen Z and millennials. He said Schwab's retention rate around wealth transfers is "extremely high." On the 4Q25 call (January 2026), he said Gen Z comprised nearly a third of new retail client accounts opened in 2025, and nearly 60% are under 40.
adjacent.differs_because: These are Schwab's figures, not Edward Jones's. Edward Jones does not disclose a comparable younger-client mix in the evidence provided.

adjacent.text: The 3Q25 10-Q (published 2025-11-07) says financial advisor attrition was 6.1%, including a rise in departures of advisors with tenure of five years or less.
adjacent.differs_because: This concerns advisor attrition, not the acquisition or retention of younger clients.

gaps.what: Edward Jones's client age mix, share of clients under 40, and new-client or retention results for younger clients are not disclosed in the evidence provided.

gaps.what: Specific products or advisory services for younger clients, and the launch status and features of the Next Generation digital platform, are not described in the evidence provided.
